assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) are a textbook case of a measurement technique that moved the frontier of precision by orders of magnitude, with fractional uncertainties at the 1e-18 level. They open fundamental-physics tests (variation of constants, dark-matter searches), relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the SI second. This matches the view that progress is limited by how well we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept (2001-2003) and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Ye brought the system to extreme accuracy and coherence and drove the many-body and systematics advances. The two-name configuration is clean. The list does not include other important contributors (for example Ye's JILA collaborators, other national-lab groups, or the earlier ion-clock and comb work already recognized), so the credit is reasonable but not exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL and others) have reproduced and compared clocks at the 1e-18 level. The interpretation is stable, and the redefinition of the second is under active discussion. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Prior Nobel recognition of frequency combs and ion-trap work (Hall, Haensch, Wineland) may be seen as having already covered part of this territory.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI-second redefinition as a marker of impact.
I am relying on my own recollection of the priority between Katori's proposal and parallel suggestions, and have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV-center spins in diamond created a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, electric fields, temperature and strain. It has spread into biology, materials science (including imaging in condensed matter) and quantum networks. From a measurement standpoint this is a clear example of a method that opens new ways of observing nature, with a long chain from single-defect detection to practical devices.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Gruber (1997) first detected single NV centres optically and magnetically; Jelezko and Wrachtrup (2004) demonstrated coherent control and coupling to nearby nuclear spins; Lukin's group contributed key theory and experiments on nanoscale magnetometry and quantum registers. The three names are a plausible configuration. Other contributors (for example Awschalom, Hanson and Balasubramanian, who are not in the credited set) mean the allocation is not unique.
assessment.maturity: The result is confirmed by many groups and has produced commercial quantum sensors. The field is still diversifying, but the basic discoveries are two decades old and robust.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many groups, and the credited list omits some strong contributors.
Lukin also appears on other candidate lines, which affects how the committee may want to distribute recognition.
Sensing applications are still maturing relative to the underlying spin control.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms has become a precision-measurement platform for gravity, gravity gradients, the fine-structure constant, tests of the equivalence principle and inertial navigation. The coherent beam-splitter concepts and the realization of atom interferometers are original and have had a lasting impact on measurement science. This is a method that has enabled a wide set of other work.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer and early theory), Pritchard (the first atom interferometers and the grating-based work with Mach-Zehnder geometry) and Kasevich (with Chu, the light-pulse atom interferometer and high-precision gravimetry) are the central names in the supplied credit. Steven Chu is not in the credited set and he already received a Nobel Prize for cooling, which complicates how the credit would be framed. The allocation among the three is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with commercial gravimeters and large-scale (long-baseline) devices being built. Independent confirmation is extensive. Interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Overlap with already-recognized laser cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation prizes.
Priority and allocation among Bordé, Pritchard, Chu and Kasevich are contestable.
Large-scale fundamental-physics applications (gravitational-wave detection, dark-matter searches) are still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics created the architecture (the transmon plus microwave resonator and dispersive readout) that underlies essentially all current superconducting quantum processors. It turned cavity QED ideas into a practical device platform with high-fidelity readout and control, and it set the stage for much of the work on quantum error-correction demonstrations. Importance and clarity are high.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues proposed the architecture in 2004, with Girvin and Schoelkopf part of that theory team; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling experimentally in the same year. I propose Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Blais as the experimental and theory core, leaving Girvin out; this is a judgment call and could reasonably go either way. The 2025 prize to macroscopic quantum tunneling in superconducting circuits already touched this platform, which affects how the committee would frame an additional award.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed by many groups and by industrial programs, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, though the committee might consider whether recent related awards leave enough room.
uncertainties: The proximity to the recent superconducting-circuits prize may reduce room for a related award soon.
The theory-versus-experiment split of credit (Girvin versus Blais) is not obvious.
The scale-up to useful fault-tolerant machines is not yet shown, though that is not required for the basic discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade yields strong, switchable interactions between neutral atoms, and optical-tweezer arrays have turned this into a programmable platform for quantum simulation and computing with hundreds of qubits. It has produced demonstrations of many-body phases, high-fidelity gates and early error-correction experiments. Strong on experimental demonstration and on enabling other work.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and co-workers proposed the Rydberg blockade for quantum information (2001), Saffman contributed gate proposals and experiments, Browaeys and Grangier demonstrated blockade between single atoms (2009), and Lukin's group with Greiner and others built the large programmable arrays. The list has four names and the prize allows three; leaving out Grangier is a judgment call, and Jaksch and Zoller (who are not in the credited set) are historically relevant to the blockade proposal.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing, with multiple independent groups and companies, but the interpretation of what the platform will ultimately do is still evolving. Slightly early compared with the older candidates, though the core results are strongly confirmed.
uncertainties: Credit is split between the theory proposals and the later array demonstrations.
The field is advancing quickly, so a few years more may clarify the leading contributions.
Lukin appears across several candidate lines.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Titanium-sapphire gain media and the passive mode-locking methods (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors) made reliable femtosecond lasers a standard tool. They are the foundation of much of ultrafast spectroscopy, frequency-comb metrology, multiphoton microscopy and attosecond science, so the work has enabled a very large body of other results. The measurement-enabling character is strong.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed the Ti:sapphire laser material and laser (1982), Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking in 1990-91 (Spence, Kean and Sibbett), and Keller invented the SESAM for stable passive mode-locking. This is a plausible three-person split. Chirped-pulse amplification already received a prize (2018), and some ultrafast areas have been recognized, so the committee may be wary of a partial overlap.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous. The only question is whether it is perceived as an enabling technology of an already-honored field rather than a distinct discovery.
uncertainties: Overlap with prizes for CPA, frequency combs and attosecond pulses.
Whether the committee considers an engineering-driven laser technology to be physics discovery in the Nobel sense.
Attribution details between Kerr-lens work and the earlier Ti:sapphire development are from my memory and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters and single-site readout (quantum gas microscopes), enabling observation of the superfluid-Mott transition, antiferromagnetic correlations and out-of-equilibrium dynamics. It created quantum simulation as an experimental discipline. The experimental demonstrations are careful and influential across condensed matter and AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) provided the theoretical proposal for Bose-Hubbard physics in lattices, Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott-insulator experiment (2002) and developed the microscope, Cirac contributed to the simulation concepts. The credited list has four names, so one must be left out; Cirac is excluded here though he overlaps with candidate B031. Jaksch is not credited, so the theory credit is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely reproduced, though the ultimate scientific payoff (solving open Hubbard-model questions such as d-wave superconductivity) has not yet been achieved. Recognition is reasonable but could be seen as slightly early on that point.
uncertainties: Open question whether the simulators have yet answered a problem inaccessible to classical methods.
Overlap in the credited names with B031, so the committee must choose how to allocate Cirac and Zoller.
Missing theory credit for those not on the list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and entanglement-based schemes) founded quantum cryptography, gave a concrete application of quantum mechanics to information security, and motivated large experimental programs including fiber and satellite links. Conceptually clear and original, with substantial influence on quantum information science. The 2022 prize recognized entanglement experiments underpinning much of this area, so the committee would need to articulate what is distinct.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84 (1984), which is the decisive contribution. Ekert independently proposed an entanglement-based protocol in 1991. Giving the prize to Bennett and Brassard alone is clean but leaves Ekert's claim unresolved; a three-person split is also plausible. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not in the credited set.
assessment.maturity: The concept is old and well established, and implementations are commercial, but the practical security of real devices (side channels, finite-key effects) is still debated. Experimental maturity is mixed compared with the metrology-type candidates.
uncertainties: As a proposal-driven contribution, it rests on later experiments by others for its demonstration.
Unresolved relative credit for Ekert and for Wiesner.
Practical security and deployment limits of real QKD systems.
